title: Which sequence space does it live in?

prereqs.why: The three spaces are defined by three convergence conditions, and the whole exercise is deciding which hold.
The three conditions are the infinite versions of the sum, the root-sum-of-squares and the maximum.

statement:
Write

$$\ell^1 = \Bigl\{x : \sum_{n\ge1} |x_n| < \infty \Bigr\},\quad
\ell^2 = \Bigl\{x : \sum_{n\ge1} |x_n|^2 < \infty \Bigr\},\quad
\ell^\infty = \Bigl\{x : \sup_{n} |x_n| < \infty \Bigr\}.$$

Match each sequence on the left to the description of its membership on the
right.

One of the descriptions on the right fits none of them — and in fact fits no
sequence at all. Working out why is part of the exercise.
hints: Take the three conditions in order of strength. Which of them implies which?
For $x_n = 1/n$: $\sum 1/n$ is the harmonic series and $\sum 1/n^2$ converges. For $x_n = 1/\sqrt n$: $\sum 1/n^{1/2}$ and $\sum 1/n$ both diverge.
A sequence whose terms are absolutely summable must have terms tending to zero, so it is bounded. That rules one of the descriptions out entirely.

right: In none of the three: the terms are not even bounded.
In all three: the terms are absolutely summable, and that forces the other two conditions.
In $\ell^\infty$ and in neither of the others, because the terms do not tend to zero at all.
In $\ell^2$ and in $\ell^\infty$ but not in $\ell^1$: the squares are summable, the terms themselves are not.
In $\ell^\infty$ and in neither of the others, because the squares sum like the harmonic series.
In $\ell^1$ and in $\ell^2$ but not in $\ell^\infty$.
